qa.q: (Kahoot) Metoprolol lowers blood pressure partly by reducing…
qa.a: Heart rate, contractility and renin release (β₁ blockade in the heart and kidney). (Answer not read aloud; from slide 23.)

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which concern is especially important with propranolol?
qa.a: Bronchospasm — propranolol is non-cardioselective, blocking β₁ and β₂.

qa.q: (Kahoot) A patient taking prazosin should be taught about…
qa.a: First-dose orthostatic hypotension from the massive vasodilation — prazosin is an alpha-1 blocker (tamsulosin blocks the alpha-1s in the prostate).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Carvedilol lowers blood pressure through which two effects?
qa.a: ↓ Cardiac output (β₁ blockade) and ↓ systemic vascular resistance (α₁ blockade). (Answer not read aloud; from slide 25.)

qa.q: (Kahoot) Abruptly stopping clonidine can cause…
qa.a: Rebound hypertension — with any sympatholytic, "we don't want to abruptly stop."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Hydralazine can trigger reflex tachycardia because…
qa.a: Blood pressure falls and the baroreceptor reflex responds with ↑ heart rate.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which effect is characteristic of amlodipine?
qa.a: Peripheral edema — the dihydropyridine CCB's "kind of benign edema": normally edema is a concern, but with this class we expect it.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Why use caution combining verapamil and metoprolol?
qa.a: Both decrease heart rate, contractility and AV-node conduction — together they really suppress the heart.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Why is cough less common with losartan than lisinopril?
qa.a: ARBs don't increase bradykinin; ACE normally breaks bradykinin down, so ACE inhibitors let it build up. (She moved on; from slide 39.)

qa.q: (student asked) Does impaired pacemaker activity mean the SA node?
qa.a: Yes — "we're talking about the pacemaker itself of the heart, that SA node." (Question reconstructed from her answer.)

qa.q: (student asked) Where does the clot go in AFib?
qa.a: It forms in the atria, gets pumped out through the ventricle and can lodge in many places (e.g. the renal artery); the most dangerous is the brain → stroke. Tiny clots can show up as little marks in the fingernails.

qa.q: (student asked) Do patients feel atrial fibrillation?
qa.a: Not always — if the ventricular beats stay fairly regular and cardiac output holds, they may not feel it, especially older clients with comorbidities. The catch: after more than 24 hours in AFib you can't simply cardiovert, because a clot has almost certainly formed and the shock could break it free — anticoagulate first.

qa.q: (student asked) Why the left side, particularly the left atrial appendage?
qa.a: The appendage is a little out-pouching of the left atrium that makes it much easier for blood to clot there. Right-sided clots happen too (and go to the lungs), but far less often.

qa.q: (student asked) Could sustained SVT cause blood to back up?
qa.a: "It could" — if it's sustained, blood backs up and you'd see signs and symptoms of heart failure; over a long time, hypertrophy. But SVT shouldn't be allowed to go on that long.

qa.q: (student asked) Can you stimulate the vagus nerve through the neck?
qa.a: Yes, but it carries danger: with carotid plaques you could break one free, and pressing on the carotid interrupts blood flow to the brain.

qa.q: (student asked) Can recurring SVT be fixed for good?
qa.a: Rate control comes first, but if studies find where the abnormal impulse starts, ablation (heat, freezing or laser) can destroy the misbehaving tissue and "can work very nicely." Unstable → cardioversion.

qa.q: (student asked) Are patients awake when they get adenosine?
qa.a: Usually, unless the SVT knocked them out. They feel everything slow down and stop, then feel better once the rate is no longer racing — and it's nerve-wracking for the nurse giving it too.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Why does atrial fibrillation increase stroke risk?
qa.a: "When blood stops flowing or slows down, it starts to clot" — blood stasis plus turbulence.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which finding is characteristic of atrial flutter?
qa.a: Regular but incredibly fast atrial activity — the sawtooth pattern ("good").

qa.q: (Kahoot) [Adenosine] can terminate some SVTs by…
qa.a: Briefly blocking AV-node conduction, which interrupts the AV node–dependent reentry circuit. (The drug name is garbled on the recording and the answer wasn't read aloud; from slide 62.)

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which treatment is essential for ventricular fibrillation?
qa.a: VF is cardiac arrest — electrical activity but no meaningful contraction — so immediate CPR and unsynchronized defibrillation (from slide 53).

qa.q: (Kahoot) What is the primary medication treatment for torsades de pointes?
qa.a: Magnesium. "The rest of them you don't need to know except for adenosine for SVT and magnesium for torsades."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat indicates…
qa.a: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I — the PR gets longer, longer, longer, until eventually a beat is dropped.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which antiarrhythmic class primarily blocks potassium channels?
qa.a: Class III (amiodarone) — "good, good."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which toxicity is important with long-term amiodarone?
qa.a: Pulmonary fibrosis — plus liver toxicity; "the big ones that we worry about."

qa.q: (Kahoot) How should adenosine be administered for SVT?
qa.a: Rapid IV push followed immediately by a saline flush, with continuous ECG monitoring. (From slide 63 and her demonstration.)

qa.q: If a DVT breaks free from the leg, where does it go?
qa.a: She answered: up to the lungs — a pulmonary embolus; if it's large enough it can kill you, and it's one of the main causes of death in hospitalized patients.

qa.q: (student asked) Why don't primary care offices just screen everyone with an EKG?
qa.a: "I don't know" — she guessed many offices don't have the machine and it's an additional expense.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Cardiac tamponade decreases cardiac output primarily by…
qa.a: Decreasing ventricular filling — the fluid-filled, stiff sac squeezes the heart, so stroke volume and CO fall. (Answer not read aloud; from slide 67.)

qa.q: (Kahoot) [Valve] stenosis primarily causes…
qa.a: Pressure overload (regurgitation causes volume overload). (Reconstructed from a garbled stretch; from slides 68 and 80.)

qa.q: (Kahoot) [A question on] Virchow's triad
qa.a: Venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability. (Reconstructed from a garbled stretch; from slide 74.)

qa.q: (Kahoot) In infective endocarditis, vegetations can cause…
qa.a: Embolization → stroke or systemic infarction (and valve destruction → regurgitation → heart failure). (Answer not read aloud; from slide 78.)
